title: Nirmal Purja and Nine Climbers Missing After Avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak
excerpt: The record-breaking Nepalese mountaineer known for Netflix's '14 Peaks' led a 10-person expedition that has been out of contact since a snowslide struck around midday Thursday.
body:
• World-famous Nepalese climber Nirmal "Nims" Purja and nine other mountaineers are missing after an avalanche struck Pakistan's Broad Peak around midday Thursday.
  • The team includes five Nepalese climbers, a Pakistani mountaineer, an American climber from Texas, and nationals from Oman and China.
  • The Alpine Club of Pakistan has mobilized helicopter support and rescue resources, but weather conditions are complicating the operation.
  • Purja, a former British special forces soldier, is best known for climbing all 14 peaks above 8,000 meters in just over six months — a feat chronicled in the Netflix documentary "14 Peaks."

Avalanche Strikes at 26,400 Feet

An avalanche tore through a climbing expedition on Pakistan's Broad Peak on Thursday afternoon, leaving 10 mountaineers — including record-breaking Nepalese climber Nirmal Purja — out of contact and feared missing, the Alpine Club of Pakistan confirmed.

https://x.com/EverestToday/status/2082970071320912287

The snowslide struck the 10-person team around midday as they trekked on the 8,047-meter peak in the Karakoram mountain range, the world's 12th tallest mountain. The entire team has been unreachable since the avalanche, according to the Alpine Club's statement.

"Every possible effort is being made to ensure that helicopter support and all available rescue resources are mobilized at the earliest opportunity, subject to weather and operational conditions."

— Alpine Club of Pakistan

Who Is on the Mountain

The expedition, led by the 43-year-old Purja, consists of five Nepalese mountaineers, Pakistani climber Sohail Sakhi from Hunza, American climber Mallory Geis of Texas, one Omani climber, a Chinese national identified as Mr. Wang, and one other foreign climber, according to the Alpine Club.

Geis had been joining Sakhi on his Broad Peak expedition, according to a post by trekking company Moving Mountains on Instagram.

Weather Warnings Preceded the Disaster

Experienced climbers had raised concerns about conditions on Broad Peak in the days before the avalanche. Napier Sandford Fuller, a 53-year-old high-altitude climber who led an expedition up the same peak the previous week, told the New York Post he had feared trouble.

"It had been raining every day, which means that at high altitude, it would have been snowing. I remember thinking, they're going to have a hell of a problem because if it's raining for a week straight, it's going to have a huge snow load on that mountain."

— Napier Sandford Fuller, mountaineer

Major General Irfan Arshad, president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan, said the organization was working closely with government authorities to coordinate the rescue effort. Helicopters and emergency resources were being deployed to the remote mountainside as quickly as conditions allowed.

A Climbing Legend

Purja, widely known as "Nims" or "Nimsdai," served 16 years in the British military — first with the Brigade of Gurkhas and later with the Special Boat Service, the Royal Navy's special forces unit. He was awarded an MBE by Queen Elizabeth II in 2018 for exceptional military service in high-risk environments.

He became a global figure in mountaineering in 2019, when he climbed all 14 of the world's peaks above 8,000 meters in just six months and six days — a record at the time. He was also the first person to summit Mount Everest, Lhotse, and Makalu within 48 hours. In 2021, he led the first winter ascent of K2, alongside a team of nine other Nepalese climbers.

His feats were chronicled in the hit Netflix documentary "14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible," which brought him widespread recognition beyond the climbing community.

What's Next

Search and rescue operations are set to intensify as weather permits. Broad Peak, standing at 8,051 meters, is regarded as one of the most technically challenging and dangerous mountains in the world. The Karakoram range, which straddles the Pakistan-China border, has seen multiple fatalities over the decades due to avalanches, altitude sickness, and extreme weather.

The climbing community is watching closely, with tributes and messages of hope flooding social media for Purja and his team. Pakistan's climbing season typically runs from June through August, when conditions on the Karakoram's highest peaks are at their most favorable — though still perilous.
